speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have this opportunity to rise and speak on the motion before us. I commend the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) on introducing it today. As he mentioned in his opening remarks, he has been a Member of the House for a long time and has spoken on similar Bills or motions over the years. The political rights-indeed, the basic civil rights-of public servants have been a question of importance to me and to other Hon. Members on this side of the House for some period of time. I first rose to speak on the issue in November of last year in my maiden speech when I called for the restoration of political rights for public servants. Hon. Members may know that I was the only public servant elected to this House in last year's election.
This motion raises basic questions about the essential liberties of the Canadian people; whether a group of Canadians has the right to free speech, free assembly, and the right to work peacefully and lawfully for democratic change. On the surface, it would seem that there would be no question about this, but serious objections have been raised and have dominated this discussion for more than half a century.
Those who believe it is justifiable to deprive public servants of political rights make three basic arguments, Mr. Speaker: First, the case is made that public servants must not be permitted to participate in the political process, or to speak freely about public issues because there might be a conflict between the loyalties to Party and the loyalty to the Minister. This argument suggests that any perception of such a conflict of interest would undermine public confidence in the Public Service.
The second argument suggests that if public servants have the right to participate as other citizens do in the political process, or have the right to make public comment on public issues, that this might influence the decisions they have to make as they implement Government policies. They might give preference, for example, to their political friends when letting contracts or hiring new staff.
The third argument is that public servants would use their positions as advisers to Ministers to promote their own political philosophies. How, it is argued, could Ministers be assured that the advice they receive is not motivated by partisan or other types of considerations.
These are, indeed, serious questions, Mr. Speaker, and they are not questions which those who favour restoration of political rights should casually dismiss. If public servants are to have their basic rights restored, those of us who seek this restoration must answer these objections. If they could not be answered, there would indeed be some reason to consider abrogating the basis rights of freedom of speech and affiliation. However, if reasonable arguments can be marshalled against these objections, then we must not take the dire step of depriving adult Canadians of their basic liberties.
If we look at other jurisdictions, Mr. Speaker, we see that Canada's restrictions on these civil liberties exceeds those of
most other advanced western democracies. In the United States, Great Britain, Australia, France and Sweden, public servants have the right of free public expression. Where there are restrictions on political activity, these restrictions are clearly spelled out as they are in the United States, for instance. Where there are not clearly spelled out restrictions, as in Australia, for example, public servants are given the benefit of the doubt in their permitted action. While American law does not permit public servants to run for public office, it does clearly permit them the right to express an opinion on public issues, either privately or publicly, to display political badges and stickers, to be a member of a political party and to attend political conventions, although not, interestingly enough, to be a delegate to a convention. The limitations on their actions, in other words, are also clearly spelled out.
In the United Kingdom, there is a clear delineation of political rights for different categories of public servants, running from complete freedom for some public servants in jobs of low political sensitivity, to restrictions similar to those we have in Canada for a small group of senior public servants.
The basic criteria guiding the British rule, as the Fulton Committee in the U.K., a committee dealing with the civil service, stated, was that, and I quote:
Officials should not be drawn into expressing personal views on policy matters which could be represented as in conflict with those of their Ministers.
Only Japan and the Federal Republic of Germany, among the industrialized democracies, have restrictions greater than those we have in Canada.
With the passage of legislation governing the Civil Service in 1908 and 1918, political rights of civil servants in this country were strictly limited, initially with the laudable intention of reducing the debilitating effects which unbridled patronage had created in the Public Service and throughout Canada. For 50 years thereafter these restrictions continued until the Public Service Employment Act of 1967 gave public servants the limited rights to attend political meetings, to contribute money to a political party and to request, although not to be automatically granted, a leave of absence without pay if they wished to run for public office.
The report of the Task Force on Conflict of Interest in the Public Sector which reported last year said, and I quote:
The practical effect of Section 32 of the Public Service Employment Act has been to extend virtually full political rights to roughly 90 per cent of public servants.
The remaining 10 per cent who were deprived were presumably deputy heads and senior public servants.
I must say, Mr. Speaker, that I disagree strongly with the view of the task force as expressed in that quotation. If, in fact, Canadian public servants were treated as are those in other jurisdictions and, if, where legislation describing their political rights was vague and the benefit of the doubt was given to the public servant, then what the task force suggested might be true. This Act does not spell out all the restrictions on public servants. It spells them out in really nothing more than a cursory manner. It leaves interpretation of the Act up to the Public Service Commission.
September 23, 1985

Unfortunately, for public servants, the interpretation of Section 32 of this Act has been notoriously fickle. Until last year many public servants in the National Capital Region did in fact participate in elections, working for candidates and all three political Parties represented in this House. The Public Service Commission in most cases overlooked this activity. However, outside of Ottawa, it often tended to act more severely, limiting the rights of public servants.
Federal departments governed by this Act interpreted this Act in different ways, and other federal agencies, not subject to the Act, have varied from permitting almost complete political freedom to public servants in some agencies, to putting severe limits on others. What this means, Mr. Speaker, is that some public servants have been denied rights which other public servants of equal status have been granted, and that in all cases, public servants have had their rights defined not by Parliament, the guardian of our civil liberties. Rather, these rights have been deprived by the whim of unelected officials or regulatory agencies.
Had the Task Force on the Conflict of Interest had the opportunity to consider the Public Service Commission's interpretation of Section 32-referred to by the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier in his remarks-I am convinced its members would not have said that the practical effect of Section 32 was to extend virtually full political rights to public servants. In fact, this interpretation had the practical effect of prohibiting public servants from working for political parties in any capacity. It prevented them from attending political conventions or from making public comments on public issues.
It prevented those Canadians who happen to be public servants from taking part in the simplest of tasks in connection with the last general election. The result was to force those who did decide to work for a candidate stuffing envelopes, typing letters or answering phone calls, to look over their shoulders for fear that big brother, watching from the safety of the Public Service Commission, would catch them.
The campaigns of all three of the political Parties in this House, particularly in the National Capital Region, were assisted by workers who defy this ruling. These same campaigns were harmed by the loss of many capable individuals who were forced out of the political process by fear of the Public Service Commission. I think we should be clear about this, Mr. Speaker. These were the results, not of the acts of this Parliament taking a clearly thought out and detailed decision on a fundamental issue of civil liberties, but rather the results of administrative fiat, which arose from the vagueness of an ill-defined law, a law which allows unelected officials to deprive a group of Canadians of their democratic rights.
The fickle interpretation of the Public Service Employment Act extended also to decisions as to who should be allowed to take a leave of absence to run for political office. I was a public servant who was fortunate enough to receive the permission of the Commission to run. However, other equally competent individuals who could have served all three Parties, and all Canadians in this House, have been deprived of the right even to seek the nomination of a political Party.
Public Service Employment Act
Section 32 of the Public Service Employment Act does not deal with the rights of public servants to comment on public issues in public. Limitations on freedom of expression for public servants have evolved largely through regulation by government agencies-not by legislation. The Public Service Staff Relations Board has set stringent limits on freedom of expression by public servants, banning criticisms of public policy.
It has done this even if it cannot be shown that such comments affect a public servant's effectiveness in the performance of his or her duties. The question has not become one of depriving people of their rights because it interferes with their public duties, but just depriving them of their rights.
However, we have a Charter of Rights today, enshrined in our Constitution, and this Charter guarantees everyone in Canada the freedoms of conscience, of thought, of belief, of opinion and expression. The Charter clearly says that these rights are subject only to "such reasonable limits prescribed by law as can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society." In my view, the current restrictions of Section 32 go too far to be reasonable. The law turns the basic rights of a large number of Canadians over to the whims of unelected officials. The interpretation and implementation of this law has resulted in unreasonable limitations on even the smallest and most innocuous of political activities by public servants.
If we believe that the Charter of Rights is more than just easy rhetoric, then it is clear that we cannot permit unelected administrators or regulatory agencies to define who has rights and who does not. If there are to be restrictions, the burden of denying a group of Canadians their basic rights must be borne by the elected representatives of the people, who can spell out these restrictions in detail, and after sober reflection. We must act on the principle that fundamental rights cannot be casually abrogated, least of all by officials who do not represent the public will. We must proceed on the basis that unless fundamental rights are specifically denied in law, they are retained. If we are to deny these fundamental rights, then we must specify in law what this means in practice, as other countries have done.
This is an issue which affects a large number of Canadians. Two hundred and twenty-two thousand Canadians are governed by the Public Service Employment Act, and there are more than three hundred and sixty thousand more who work in Crown agencies and the Canadian Forces, but are not governed by this Act. Of this additional number, many thousands are deprived of political rights by decisions of the agencies for which they work. The situation is getting worse, Mr. Speaker. The number of Canadians directly governed by the Public Service Commission, or its predecessor, the Civil Service Commission, and thus automatically denied their political rights, has grown by almost one hundred thousand in the last 25 years. Among the people denied these rights by the Public Service Employment Act are 90,000 women; this in a society which is just beginning to deal with the fact that women have been grossly under-represented in Canadian public life.

September 23, 1985
Public Service Employment Act
The effects on the political life of this country are huge. Two thirds of all public servants live outside of the National Capital Region, so almost every community in every constituency, in every province of this country has people who are now, or could easily be deprived of their basic rights. The effects on the political life of this city, and region and our neighbours across the Ottawa River, are profound. What we have here, Mr. Speaker, is an attempt to isolate, to render politically steril a very large number of Canadians. They have been isolated in the attempt to make them politically neutral. Some people think that doing this will ensure that Ministers receive impartial advice, notwithstanding the personal opinions of the public servants working for them. These, then are the basic arguments which have been used to justify the denial of free expression to so many Canadians.
We have seen, Mr. Speaker, that the scope of these limitations is profound. What we must ask ourselves now is, first, will these limitations have the effect we want them to have, that is rendering the Public Service completely neutral and impartial; and, second, are there no alternatives to the severe and capricious limitations now imposed? What about the argument that public servants must not participate in the political process, because this would allow them to use their official positions to promote their personal political philosophies? Are we to assume that the only people who have a political philosophy are those who are active members of a political party? Preventing party membership will not sterilize the minds of public servants. Just as there are active members of political parties, although I am sure none in this House, who have no discernible political philosophy aside from self-interest, we are all aware from recent example of just how profoundly the political philosophies of supposedly neutral public servants have affected the development of public policy.
The fact is that whether public servants belong to a political party or not, their political philosophies will remain intact. Preventing them from speaking, or from participating in the political process will not stop them from thinking. It is naive, to the point of gullibility, to assume that all political views, or even the most important political allegiances, are revealed by party membership or by outspoken public comment. It is true that the public and Ministers have rights here. They have the right not to the illusion that public servants have no political opinions. Instead, they have the right to know what those opinions are, so that they may know if those views are biasing their judgment. There is no protection for the public in a muzzled Public Service, only an increased chance for the unobstrusive influence of their personal, hidden political views. The open admission of political affiliation is the clearest guarantee that Ministers will be able to judge the motives of their public servants when they give their advice. With the restoration of political rights to public servants, and openly declared political affiliation, any public servant with active party affiliation will be constrained to behave in an objective manner when dealing with the public, to demonstrate that political bias does not exist.
Nothing in the restoration of political rights to public servants removes the burden on the Public Service of behaving in a non-partisan manner in the execution of public duties. The rules requiring non-partisan, unbiased behaviour in their dealings with the public would still apply, and might be easier to enforce, because political affiliation, and thus possible bias, would be clearer. There is nothing unethical in expressing a political opinion. The only threat to our ethical standards occurs if those opinions, whether privately held or publicly expressed, result in bias in the performance of official duties. Certainly, if there is bias in the actions of a public servant, it must be dealt with. The essential question is whether public servants will act to implement government policy in a non-partisan manner, not whether they have personal views on politics or political philosophy.
Of course, it is essential that Canadians be assured their treatment by public servants will not be coloured by their political affiliation. They should also be assured that their treatment is not affected by their sex, their race, their language, or their ethnic origin. We make every effort to restrict discrimination on these grounds. We have laws and regulations prohibiting discrimination on these grounds, not prohibiting people from having bigoted views because that is impossible, but regulations which prohibit public servants from manifesting any such views in the execution of their public functions. Those who feel they have been poorly treated by public servants have means for appeal. Political descrimination by public servants can and should be handled in the same way. If we implement some of the changes suggested by the Starr-Sharp report, then there will be additional mechanisms in place which can review the behaviour of public servants to ensure that political bias is no more prevalent than linguistic, racial or sexual bias. We expect the Public Service to treat members of the public with the dignity they deserve, regardless of sex, race, age, language or ethnic origin-or political affiliation. We must treat public servants with the same dignity, the same recognition of their rights, as long as they do their job.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I say that I support the suggestions of the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier and, as 1 said before in this House, the recommendation of the D'Avignon Committee which he referred to and which would divide the Public Service basically on the British model into three categories, giving full political rights to most public servants, particularly those unionized, limited political rights to those in the centre, and basically status quo for those at senior levels.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   PUBLIC SERVICE EMPLOYMENT ACT SUGGESTED AMENDMENT RESPECTING GREATER PARTICIPATION IN POLITICAL PROCESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate. It is now the third time the matter has been debated in the last six months in the House of Commons. I hope that early action will be taken by the Government to ensure that Private Members' Hour can be devoted to other subjects besides the subject of political rights. Because the Hon. Member for Ottawa West (Mr. Baubney) has spoken eloquently on this subject, this time the subject has been proposed by the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), supported by myself as the Hon. Member for
September 23, 1985

Ottawa Centre, it indicates there is all Party support for the concept of implementing the promises made by all three Parties on political rights. The message should surely now be conveyed and thus 1 hope the Parliamentary Secretary will convey to the Minister that all sides are getting a bit impatient about delays when action could and should have been taken previously.
I commend the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier for introducing this subject. It is in my recollection the first time the matter has been raised in this House by a Liberal Member since the Liberals promised in the election campaign of 1980 to support the concept of political rights for people in the Public Service. The Liberals forgot that promise when they were in office from 1980 to 1984. It is my great regret that when the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong) put forward specific legislation to provide political rights for people in the Public Service, it was my predecessor, the Member for Ottawa Centre, a Liberal, who was instrumental on more than one occasion in talking out that legislation and indicating that far from supporting the position taken by the Member for Ottawa-Vanier and apart from the right to put up lawn signs, he did not think that people in the Public Service should have increased political rights.
The Liberals have been equivocal on this. I hope and trust that the Member for Ottawa-Vanier is expressing the views of all in his Party. I certainly welcome the commitment that he has made on a number of occasions now that he is sitting in Opposition.
I would comment on one thing he mentioned in his presentation. He stated that he favours the D'Avignon Report approach in terms of providing for political rights for members of the Public Service, but doing so on a qualified basis. I would say that a qualified basis, which puts the rights of any Public Service employee at question, that they must have proof or possibly risk being challenged, is a situation which could still leave many people in the Public Service feeling insecure and unsure of their rights. That is why I have come to the view that as far as members of bargaining units are concerned, they should unequivocally enjoy full political rights. We can rely on them to be responsible in exercising those rights should they happen to be in a position which has any sensitivity, but they should unequivocally enjoy the same political rights as any other person in Canadian society.
A qualified approach, similar to the D'Avignon Report might conceivably then apply to the 10 or 15 per cent of members of the Public Service of Canada who are in managerial, supervisory or exempt positions. I would like to avoid a situation where that qualified business of "do you have rights or not" would apply to everybody, including a truckdriv-er, a carpenter, a secretary or a statistical clerk in Stats-Canada. I would like to see that avoided.
There is real urgency in this debate. I think the mandate of any Government begins to unwind after its first year, and we have had that now.
A firm promise was made on this subject by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who was then Leader of the Opposi-
Public Service Employment Act
tion during the course of the election campaign. He was quite unequivocal in terms of making his promises. It seems to me that if this matter is allowed to wait for too long, Mr. Speaker, we could face the situation where the promise will be forgotten. The now Prime Minister said during the summer of 1984:
We believe that this matter should be addressed by an all-Party parliamentary committee in consultation with Public Service organizations and we believe the situation can be quickly resolved.
Further he stated that the restrictions on Public Service political activity, and I quote:
-are unnecessary and likely not justifiable under the terms of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
I do not agree with the Prime Minister on every point but I agreed with his judgment at that time. I welcomed the promise he made. When I stood for Parliament in my riding of Ottawa Centre this was a key issue among my constituents. I made a personal pledge to continue to work for legislation to ensure that Section 32 of the Public Service Employment Act is changed and that members of the Public Service of Canada do enjoy full political rights. I made this commitment not just to my constituents but also to people in the Public Service across Canada.
We are not just talking about 220,000 people who are governed by the Public Service Employment Act. The PSCA has influence far beyond that. The Member for Ottawa West mentioned that employees of Crown corporations and people in National Defence bring the total number to something around
600,000	who are tinged or affected by the Public Service Employment Act. He might have mentioned that close to one worker in every four in Canada works in some level of Government, for a Crown corporation or for some other quasi-governmental body. Federal legislation in this, as in other matters affecting labour standards for public employees, has an effect on legislation affecting provincial and other Government employees as well. We are talking about a potential impact that could touch 2.5 million workers across the country, depending on what kind of leadership is being offered by the federal Government.
As far as my own concern about this, in the first place I strongly support providing full political rights for public employees. I have done this for a long time. I first began raising this issue when I was an Ontario MPP 12 or 13 years ago. My first private Members' Bill on the subject was introduced in the Ontario legislature around 1974 and debated around that time, Mr. Speaker. I have been raising this issue in whatever forum I could because I think it is important that people in the Public Service not be treated as second class citizens.
More recently, this matter was raised on April 15 in a resolution I put forward to have the matter of political rights referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates and debated in this House. I regret to say that while it was debated, it was subsequently talked out by Members of the Progressive Conservative Party. The resolution at that time read:

September 23, 1985
Public Service Employment Act
That the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates be empowered to study the question of granting to federal public employees the full political participation enjoyed by other Canadians and, that the Committee report its finding to the House no later than June 28, 1985.
On September 13, I took the opportunity to raise the matter anew although I could not debate it. My colleague from Regina East debated it on my behalf representing the New Democratic Party. Again the matter was bogged down when Government Members suggested that the date we suggested be shifted to was perhaps inappropriate.
I raised this matter in early April in connection with the Ontario election. A number of people who are federal public employees were finding that the lack of political rights was causing them problems. One, a Transport Canada employee, has subsequently had to resign his position on the executive of a local riding association at the risk of otherwise losing his job. When the Parliamentary Secretary suggested, as I understand it, on September 13 that this was not really a matter of grave urgency because we had four years to sort it out, or three years to the next election, I wished I could have risen then to remind him that many provincial elections will take place in a very short time. All three prairie provinces are expecting to have elections within the next year or so. Quebec may be calling an election within a month of the election of its new Premier and leader of the Parti Quebecois. Ontario could have an election at any time. Certainly after two years from last May one would imagine that open season on an election in Ontario is going to be present. Federal employees working in provinces representing two-thirds of our population could find themselves still circumscribed in elections that are due to come very shortly.
This matter is urgent and cannot wait to the very end of the mandate. Let me say to the Parliamentary Secretary, and through him to his Minister, that if the Government is prepared to bring forward legislation, which can be debated here and referred to a legislative committee, by all means let it be done. Let it be done now. I am prepared to work on it. I am sure my colleagues from Ottawa-Vanier and Ottawa West are. Others have expressed support. Do not put us off by promises of early action, such as 1 had from the Minister when I raised this matter in Question Period in early April, by saying he hoped to have a report to the House very soon and then use it as a means of obfuscation or delay. This matter cannot and should not wait. I say to the Government be aware as well, and I recognize that I have some potential conflict in this, that this matter is going to come up in the Federal Court of Canada in a few weeks. Over the course of the summer, Justice Department lawyers and lawyers representing four members of the Public Service Alliance and myself have been resolving the nitty-gritties of the case so that the principles about whether restrictions on political rights violate the Charter of Rights and Freedoms can be discussed and rules upon by the Federal Court of Canada. Frankly, I would prefer to see a situation wherein the Government, having made a solemn pledge in its election campaign, fulfilled that pledge by bringing forth legislation, therefore possibly making the need for a court case nugatory. I would prefer to see that. I and other people as well
have gone forward because of the fact, among other things, that the action which we had been led to expect from the Government had not yet come forward.
Recently 1 sat on the subcommittee of the Justice Committee looking at the question of equality rights. I made submissions with respect to that question and the implications of the particular section of the Charger which indicates that every individual is equal before and under the law and has the right to equal protection and equal benefit under the law without discrimination. As Hon. Members know, this is qualified only by such reasonable limits as can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society. If we legislate restrictions on senior policy analysts and Deputy Ministers, I think the courts will uphold those as being reasonable limits in a free and democratic society, but not for truck drivers, secretaries, mining inspectors in the Yukon or the vast range of people who work in the myriad employment of the Public Service of Canada.
In its brief before the equality committee, the Public Service Alliance made essentially the same points. This matter keeps coming up in one way or another because, to give them their credit, Public Service unions are not prepared this time to stand back and accept the promises made by Parties in the election campaign or to wait for something to happen. They are pressing hard. I am pressing hard. The Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier the Hon. Member for Ottawa West and other Hon. Members, particularly the Hon. Member for Gatineau (Mrs. Mailly), are concerned about the issue and are speaking positively about the need to take action to ensure that people in the Public Service are not treated in a second-class way. Of course, we now have a situation where all three Parties are in fact committed to the issue, even though the Liberal commitment is perhaps somewhat more ambiguous.
The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) initiated discussions with the Public Service unions on this subject back in March or April. It is offered, as an excuse for the delay, that there were some problems in terms of misunderstandings, if I can be gentle about it, over the question of the deindexing of Public Service pensions and over the fact that the Public Service Alliance was also a political body which had some internal decisions to make about who should become the President at its convention in June. Recently I spoke with its new President, Mr. Daryl Bean, who had been involved because he was a member of the executive of the Alliance before the change of presidency as well as afterward. I learned essentially that no specific proposals had been put forward by the Government to the Public Service unions saying what it would like to do. There has been some canvassing of opinion, but it is not necessary to do canvassing because through the joint council and other means the Public Service unions have made their positions very clear. If they want it spelled out again, it can be done in 24 hours. They can give us a memo and we will get it for them; we will simply give all the briefs which they presented before.
September 23, 1985

What is needed now is a response from the Government that within a month's time or within a short period of time it will come up with specific guidelines from which legislation can in fact be drafted. The unions are ready. They are frustrated because of the inaction on the part of the Government. They are also frustrated, as I am, by the thought that this is part of a series of measures which could be traded off against action on pensions, on the master contract or something like that. I have been assured in private by the President of the Treasury Board that that is not the case and that the Government's commitment in the election campaign stands. However, the actions of the Government argue otherwise and suggest that it is in fact holding back until it gets action on these other areas. Since this is a matter of fundamental right, I say quite strongly that that is unacceptable and should not be tolerated, particularly in view of the fact that the discussions and negotiations in those other areas have taken perhaps longer than the Government initially expected.
In conclusion I would say that we need to maintain momentum on this subject. My colleagues and I are prepared to continue to give it Private Members' time and to raise it by other means in the House of Commons and in committee. If the Government indicates that it is acting now, so be it; let it go ahead. If not, we will have to find a way to maintain the momentum. My proposal in the spring that the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates look at the matter is a way of maintaining momentum. The Government rejected it at the time by talking it out.
The resolution of the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier today simply asks us in the House to reaffirm the position which all of us took through our political Parties and through our Leaders during the course of the election campaign a year ago. If we were prepared to make that affirmation a year ago, then the Government should decide at this point in time, at five to six, that no further speaker will rise. I appeal to all Hon. Members not to rise to speak to this matter but to allow it to come to a vote. At least that would give an indication of our support to the Government and reinforce its determination to act in line with the promises it made.
The resolution of the Hon. Member reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of amending the Public Service Employment Act and other related statutes in consequence thereof, in order to permit greater participation in the political process by federal public servants than is now allowed under the aforementioned statutes.
It is a weak resolution, but I think the intent would be clear if it were adopted. I call upon all Hon. Members to adopt this motion now.

subtopic: PUBLISHING INDUSTRY-PRENTICE-HALL COMPANY TAKEOVER. (B) GOVERNMENT POLICY
PUBLISHING INDUSTRY-PRENTICE-HALL COMPANY TAKEOVER. (B) GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week in the House I raised a very important question about the proposed takeover of Prentice-Hall Publishing by an American non-publishing company called Gulf and Western.
This is a rather complicated issue because it is an indirect acquisition of some of the concerns which have been raised by the publishing community having to do with the fact of a publishing company being taken over by a firm not in publishing which will not have the interests of publishing at heart, quite apart from the issue of American or Canadian control. Nevertheless, the Government has made a commitment to deal with indirect acquisitions. It has made a very firm commitment to increase Canadian control in the publishing sector. This was made by the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse) on July 6 and I very much welcomed that statement. It is a concern that in fact there really will be implementation of the principles that were declared at that time.
Let me quote from the Minister's statement and it is here. I will read it quickly:
This policy confirms the government's commitment, as enunciated in the Investment Canada Act, to maintaining Canada's cultural sovereignty and supporting the economic viability of the nation's crucially important cultural industries.
Let me continue:
In particular, the Government recognizes that the Canadian publishing industry must have opportunities to grow within its own domestic market and that foreign investment should not be allowed to jeopardize such development.
That is a very important matter in an industry which is largely under foreign control; largely under American control.
Concerning direct investment, the Minister stated, and here I am quoting again:
The Government will look with favour on proposals to establish new businesses or to acquire directly existing businesses, whather Canadian or foreign controlled, provided the investment is through a joint venture with Canadian control. For direct ecquisitions of foreign-controlled businesses, allowances will be possible if the divestiture of control to Canadians occurs within a reasonable period of (two years) at a fair market price.
Indirect acquisitions will be considered case by case, and again that is a question of divestiture.
The Government's policy is very clear. What we are concerned about is why it is not acting. This question of Prentice-Hall has been before the Government for nearly a year and there have been extensive delays in dealing with it.
I note that there are three other cases of a similar nature before Investment Canada: Ginn and Company; Copp Clark Pitman and New American Library.
The pressure from the arts community in the meantime is mounting. Let me quote from concerns which have been raised I think very cogently by the Association of Canadian Publishers. The Association of Canadian Publishers now looks forward to a directive by the Government which calls for the divestiture of these companies to Canadian owners. They are saying "act", and I think that is pretty clear.
The Writers' Union of Canada also has noted in terms of the subject matter why we need this control. Canadians have their own history. We have our own culture and we have our own view of others. Let me quote from their submission; "Only Canadian originated books (rather than Canadianized versions of American or British or French texts) can express those points of view and make them part of the consciousness of every Canadian".
It is a really important matter, Mr. Speaker. What we look forward to is a publishing industry in which textbooks which are the most lucrative part would also be Canadian originated, and that is not what is happening. We have companies like Prentice-Hall and others which we would like to have controlled by Canada so that the textbook publishing industries which does make money can then support other Canadian ventures.
Who is subsidizing, who is publishing the Canadian books right now? I am afraid it is not these big corporations, not like Prentice-Hall and certainly not under the control of Gulf and Western. That act of publishing comes from the small Canadian companies, and let me be specific. Up to 90 per cent of Canadian books are actually being published by smaller Canadian-owned companies. Specifically, in fiction it is 88 per cent, in biography it is 92 per cent, and in art books it is 87 per cent. The small companies are subsidizing this much more difficult field of publishing by paying small salaries and wages to their workers and by providing small royalties. In a healthy situation, we would have the textbook companies Canadian owned and the infrastructure being used to subsidize the production of important books for our Canadian culture, books that will not be bestsellers. That is how publishing works in other countries.
In other countries, the moneymakers support the production of scarcer, rarer kinds of books, books which are nevertheless extremely important for cultural purposes. That is what we must have in Canada. I call on the Government to act on this policy and not to hold back on all of these other cases as well.
I might add that the book distribution situation will run into the same problem. The merger of Classic Books with W. H. Smith will reduce opportunities for Canadian authors to have their books put on the market. We do not want a policy that is mere rhetoric. What we want is action. It is important that every case reflect this policy, and that the Government be true to the policy that it has enunciated on a case-by-case basis. Mere words are not enough.

subtopic: PUBLISHING INDUSTRY-PRENTICE-HALL COMPANY TAKEOVER. (B) GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say, first of all, that when the Investment Canada Act was still in the draft stage earlier this year, the Government clearly stated the importance it attached to the cultural sector. In fact, it demonstrated its awareness of sensitive areas in this sector in two sections of the Act.
September 23, 1985

First, Section 15. As the Hon. Member is aware, investments made by non-Canadians with a view to acquiring directly, in Canada, a business with assets of less than $5 million, or with a view to taking control, indirectly, of a business with assets of less than $50 million or with the intention of establishing a new business in this country, are not generally subject to review. The only exception to this rule has to do with investors who are associated with Canada's cultural heritage or national identity. The Government reserves the right to review such cases.
There are four sectors where the investment must be compatible with Canada's cultural heritage or national identity. Here they are: the publication, distribution or sale of books, magazines, periodicals or newspapers, either in printed form or readily assimilated by a processing machine; the production, distribution, sale or presentation of films or video materials; the production, distribution, sale or presentation of audio or video musical recordings; the edition, distribution of sale or musical compositions, either in printed form or readily assimilated by a processing machine.
Mr. Speaker, the second part of the Act which attests to our very special conviction in this field can be found under Section 20.
Section 20 lists the factors to be considered to decide whether or not an investment will likely be of significant benefit to Canada.
Subsection (<?) of Section 20 requires the Government to take into account the compatibility of the investment with national industrial, economic and cultural policies, taking into consideration industrial, economic and cultural policy objectives enunciated by the Government or Legislature of any province likely to be significantly affected by the investment.
During oral question period last September 17, when the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) asked the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion whether the takeover of the Canadian publishing firm Prentice-Hall would be permitted, the Minister explained that the administrators had informed him that they would like some time to weigh the communications policy that his colleague, the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse), made public some time ago. The Minister added: "Of course, we have facilitated their deliberations by giving them more time."
Mr. Speaker, I would now like to review the policy of the Canadian Government as concerns the Canadian book publishing industry.
Last July 6, the Minister of Communications announced this policy which states that: The Government feels that the existence of a vigourous book publishing and distribution industry controlled by Canadians is essential if this sector is to play its full role in the social and cultural life of
Adjournment Debate
Canada. The book publishing and distribution industry must benefit from policies aimed at protecting our cultural sovereignty, just as the newspapers, periodicals and broadcasting industries must do.
As concerns direct investments, according to the Minister, the Government will consider favourably any proposal to establish a new business or to acquire an existing business, whether it is controlled by Canadian or foreign interests, if this investment is projected for a joint venture under Canadian control.
In the case of the takeovers involving companies under foreign control, such transactions could be allowed if it is expected that Canadians will take control within a reasonable time, namely within two years, and at a fair market price. The Minister concluded that this policy is reflected in practice by the commitment made by this Government in the Act to establish Investment Canada to safeguard cultural sovereignty and support the financial position of cultural industries which play a vital role in our collective life. More particularly, the Government recognizes that the Canadian publishing industry must have the means to ensure its growth on the Canadian domestic market and that foreign investment must not prejudice this development.

subtopic: TRUST COMPANIES-PIONEER TRUST-PLIGHT OF UNINSURED DEPOSITORS. (B) UNINSURED INCOME AVERAGING CERTIFICATES
TRUST COMPANIES-PIONEER TRUST-PLIGHT OF UNINSURED DEPOSITORS. (B) UNINSURED INCOME AVERAGING CERTIFICATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 2,
I asked the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) two questions. I asked her whether she was still negotiating with the Minister of Finance of the Province of Saskatchewan for federal government assistance to help bail out the uninsured depositors of Pioneer Trust of Regina which went into liquidation. She did not really have too much to say in the way of an answer. I then suggested to her in a supplementary question that financial institutions were falling down like ten pins. I pointed out that the CDIC stamp was placed on income averaging certificates, suggesting that they were covered by CDIC insurance when, in fact, they were not covered. I indicated that there should be some federal Government responsibility for those accounts.
At the time of my asking the question the Minister was quite incensed at my remark with respect to financial institutions falling down like ten pins. She claimed it was an irresponsible statement and added:
I can tell you right now that financial institutions in this country are not falling like then pins, and 1 am producing results.
Since April 2, we have seen the Canadian Commercial Bank go under, the CCB mortgage investment go under, Northland is on the verge of going under and Western Capital Trust has gone under. Some estimates are that this will cost some $4 billion, either to CDIC or to the Government directly. Admittedly, from hindsight, I claim that financial institutions have been crashing around the Minister's ears since that time.

September 23, 1985
Adjournment Debate
The point is that I am not happy with the Minister's answer. How much responsibility does the federal Government accept for the uninsured depositors of Pioneer Trust? Hon. Members will remember that the Government did bring in legislation and that some federal money has gone to uninsured depositors of Pioneer Trust. I assume, and I hope the Parliamentary Secretary will make this clear today, that the federal Government considered it had some responsibility because there were these averaging certificates of over five years which had the CDIC stamp of approval.
It is important, Mr. Speaker, that the Government quite explicitly explains to the House and to the public when it accepts responsibility and when it does not. It should be clear when it is going to bail out uninsured depositors and when it is not. I have asked the Minister this question in committees and on various occasions and I will continue to do that in the days and weeks ahead.
There seems to be, Mr. Speaker, no clear policy. One day the Government decides to bail out the uninsured depositors, as it has done with the Canadian Commercial Bank and as it is apparently committed to do if Northland should go under. The Government had a partial commitment to Pioneer and there are other financial institutions which have gone under like Western Capital Trust in which the uninsured depositors have not been bailed out at all. I have received phone calls and representations from people who have lost money. They were uninsured depositors in these various trust companies and financial institutions and they are hopping mad. They ask me why the Government is bailing out foreign depositors in the CCB and not them.
I believe it is important, Mr. Speaker, that the Government, as soon as possible, lay before the public of Canada what its policies are, when it will bail out uninsured depositors and when it will not. I think it is important for depositors and for financial institutions in this country to know the answer to that question. In particular, Mr. Speaker, for my own personal interest as well, and for the record, I reiterate my question: Did the Government bail out in part uninsured depositors in Pioneer Trust because it felt it had some responsibility because of the lack of regulation and enforcement of CDIC with respect to Pioneer Trust during its years in operation and, particularly, concerning the CDIC stamp on forwarding averaging annuity certificates which were really not covered by the Deposit Insurance Corporation?

speakeroldname: Mr. Claude Lanthier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: TRUST COMPANIES-PIONEER TRUST-PLIGHT OF UNINSURED DEPOSITORS. (B) UNINSURED INCOME AVERAGING CERTIFICATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Pioneer Trust was plagued with serious financial problems because of the high percentage of outstanding mortgages in its loan portfolio. The company voluntarily wound up and a liquidation order was issued on February 15, 1985.
Shortly after the Pioneer Trust liquidation order, the Hon. Barbara McDougall, our capable Minister of State for Finance
became interested in the situation of the 650 or so guaranteed income-averaging certificates issued for a period of more than five years, and therefore uninsured by the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation.
Our able Minister was mainly concerned with the many representations received from holders of such certificates, who submitted that they were not aware their investments were not covered by deposit insurance.
The Minister's concerns with the circumstances relating to those guaranteed income averaging certificate holders led her to conclude with the Saskatachewan Governemnt a special arrangement compensating the uninsured depositors, and to introduce the legislation needed to enact such an arrangement.
The purpose of the legislation was to grant the Minister authority to take the necessary steps to have payments made to the holders of income averaging certificates for up to the $60,000 limit that would have been applicable had those certificates been insured. In other words, the purpose was for the Canadian Government to contribute to the package for compensating the uninsured depositors of Pioneer Trust up to an amount shifting them to the position they believed in good faith they were in, namely up to the well-known $60,000 limit.
The Province of Saskatchewan assumed responsibility for all payments amounting to $60,000 and over, owed under the guaranteed income average certificates. Moreover, the Saskatchewan Government also undertook to pay back principal and interests accrued at the time of liquidation order to all holders of US dollar deposits, and all holders of deposits in excess of $60,000 in savings or chequing accounts, guaranteed income certificates or registered retirement savings plans.
In view of the above circumstances, I believe it was reasonable for the Government of Canada to act in this way to make sure all holders of guaranteed income averaging certificates remain in the position they had every reason to believe they were in, namely that they were protected up to the well-known $60,000 limit. As I said, the action taken by the Canadian Government was part of a plan involving the Province of Saskatchewan as guarantor for all other uninsured deposits, including those with deposits exceeding $60,000.
Regardless of any reference to false representations, Mr. Speaker, it was a matter of being reasonable with people who acted in total good faith.

subtopic: REGIONAL INDUSTRIAL EXPANSION-EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES IN CAPE BRETON

speakeroldname: Mr. Lawrence I. O'Neil (Cape Breton Highlands-Canso):
subtopic: REGIONAL INDUSTRIAL EXPANSION-EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES IN CAPE BRETON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time to expand on a question I directed to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) last week. I have the honour of representing a constituency in Nova Scotia, Cape Breton Highlands-Canso, an area which includes some of our most impressive geography and
September 23, 1985

certainly Canadians of outstanding good judgment, having chosen to elect me to Parliament in September, 1984.
Regrettably, Mr. Speaker, it is also a region of high unemployment. This is a problem which has been faced by successive generations of my constituents. The previous Government did nothing to address the problem in a meaningful way. Our Government has taken important measures to effect full-time employment for my constituents. The Minister, in his response to my question, underscored these incentives, which include the Cape Breton tax credit and the topped-up IRDP assistance. These are generous measures. However, it appears that more must be done.
The urgency of the situation is highlighted by the fact that employees laid off from the heavy water plants really have no place to apply for new jobs at this time. I was most pleased to hear from the Minister his optimistic projections for new employment opportunities. The Minister is trying very hard and that is not disputed. Nor is the difficulty of finding a solution disputed.
This problem has been faced by successive federal and provincial Governments. However, I believe there are some other meaningful initiatives which can be taken at this time to create long-term employment. It is easy to complain that results have not been achieved. The real test of leadership for any Member of Parliament is not solely his ability to identify problems, it is also reflected in his ability to present solutions. That is the challenge which was not met by the previous Government. Today I will present a partial package which outlines some opportunities for new employment in my constituency. Exploitation of these opportunities will require the targeted expenditure of money by all levels of Government. 1 do not believe these initiatives will result in a net financial loss to the Government of Canada. Many of the people who will benefit from these expenditures presently receive incomes from one level of Government or another. In short, I am speaking about an investment by the Government of Canada, a good investment which will yield benefits for my constituents and, therefore, Canada.
In accordance with a general principle of common sense, we should first look for new economic opportunities by further utilizing our natural resources. In keeping with that bias, the following is suggested. We have an excellent environment for forest regeneration and therefore I am proposing that a greatly enhanced forest management program must be put in place. In addition to putting hundreds to work planting trees and harvesting old and decaying stock, we will be securing the raw material for the region's major industrial employer, Stora Forest Industries. We will therefore be securing existing jobs and facilitating corporate planning. Who knows, maybe a more sensible approach to our forests will mean expansion of those companies who use our forests. Perhaps another newsprint machine is possible.
We must consider the further utilization of waste wood as a fuel, perhaps to heat our institutions. Such a program would require wood chips and would put people now out of work back to work in the woods, for example. We must also view oppor-
Adjournment Debate
tunities for further expanding the Strathlorne Nursery, a source of tree seedlings which we require for an enhanced forest management program.
In the fishery we have opportunities to improve our fish quality, thereby adding to the value of our exports and permitting a greater reinvestment in our communities. We must further enhance the small crafts and harbours' programs so our fishermen will have the best possible facilities for harvesting the sea's wealth. We must be sure that our fish are further processed here and get away from exporting semi-processed product. We must examine the potential for utilizing even more species.
In the tourism industry there are greater opportunities for lengthening the season. Presently it is not uncommon for an operator to exist on a 90-day season. Surely we can improve upon this. I advocate increased spending on promotion and the enhancement of our tourism facilities and services.
The agricultural sector is growing in importance and its contribution to the economy of Antigonish County alone is $8 million. That is an impressive achievement over the last 10 or 15 years.
There are other specific measures that can be taken to achieve permanent employment. For example, I advocate the construction of a coal fired electrical generating station at the Strait of Canso. We, in Nova Scotia, have a desperate need for new electrical capacity and we must move away from the utilization of oil. In addition to putting in industry at the Strait of Canso, we will be putting miners in industrial Cape Breton to work.
I advocate the construction of an underwater institute at the Strait of Canso to complement the Nova Scotia Nautical Institute presently under construction.
I advocate the further expansion of the Strathlorne nursery, which has already been mentioned. I advocate the construction of the Grassy Island Museum in Canso, a remote part of my riding. I advocate the upgrading of the highway so that the tourism potential of this region may be further utilized.
The Cheticamp harbour must be upgraded. Millions of pounds of fish are landed there each year, much of which is trucked out. There is an opportunity for making Cheticamp the boat service centre for the Gulf region. It is a natural initiative and one that must be strongly supported. We must put capital in our shipbuilding industry.
We must further develop the potential of the Mulgrave harbour as an offshore service centre, and for international trade. We must consider the relocation of public service employment to this high unemployment region, something that we call decentralization.
These initiatives, Mr. Speaker, will require the expenditure of money, but this money will be a wise investment of our region. In promoting these we must, at all times, keep in mind the importance of being cautious and realistic.

September 23, 1985
Adjournment Debate
For decades my constituents have had false hopes held in front of them, called carrots. It is time for that to end, for results to be delivered and for us to be totally realistic.

subtopic: REGIONAL INDUSTRIAL EXPANSION-EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES IN CAPE BRETON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Cape Breton has a workforce of some 69,000 which represents 18 percent of that of Nova Scotia as a whole. Out of that figure, 14,000 are now jobless, and this accounts for a 20-percent unemployment rate. It is therefore essential that Cape Breton be the target of all industrial efforts.
The Canadian Government strategy for Cape Breton encompasses the following:
A grant package, intended to provide Cape Breton native investors and others with the incentive to apply the human and financial resources to the creation of long-term jobs;
An advisory committee to ensure the monitoring of tax incentives and recommendations on long-term job creation; and, finally,
Co-operation with the Provinces to ensure co-ordination and efficiency.
The Federal Development Bank has a program offering seminars for informing laid-off AECL employees on how to set up a business. Some of these employees have shown an interest in Cape Breton.
The RIE, the Cape Breton Development Corporation and Skita are now working together to ensure coordination in the promotion of efforts to help Cape Breton.

The Minister is looking forward to receiving the report of the Cape Breton advisory committee expected to be delivered to the federal and provincial Governments later this month. While the advisory committee is looking at long term economic development issues, the federal Government has done much to address the immediate needs of Cape Breton's unemployed. Through the ongoing and special programs of a large number of federal Departments and agencies, thousands of jobs have been created in Cape Breton to help ease the immediate crisis of unemployment.
Canada Employment and Immigration programs have created 2,500 short-term jobs in Cape Breton in 1985. Devco's coal division has put roughly 1,200 people to work on projects this year.
The Department of National Defence programs have resulted in short-term jobs for 140 Cape Breton youths. Construction at the Coast Guard college is creating about 1,200 person weeks of employment. Another Coast Guard project, particularly the wharf expansion and transit shed construction in North Sydney will create 1,500 person weeks of employment. Taken together, this will amount to about six months work for roughly 108 people.
Federal support this Fiscal year for projects under two federal provincial forestry agreements will produce over 6,240 weeks of work for Cape Bretoners to improve the Island's forest resource, the equivalent of six months work for 250 people.
Much of the work being done under the major program of CDIC and Devco will improve the infrastructure base and quality of life in Cape Breton and make the Island more attractive to industries capable of creating long-term jobs. This Government will help Cape Breton.
